videos.script: Every table in Ana's warehouse has a name, and every column has a type. Neither says what it means. {{columns}} Does net sales include shipping? Is the date the day of the order, or the day of payment? Lesson 11 needed a meeting to find out, and three numbers came out of it. {{question}} A field dictionary writes the answer down, once, next to each column: what it means, in which unit, where it comes from, and whether it describes a person. {{dictionary}} Ana keeps the descriptions in the database itself, as comments, and writes a test that fails on any column without one. {{test}} Ninety-one columns fail the first time. Then the test passes, and a dictionary is generated from the comments instead of written beside them. {{generate}} The same file says which columns are personal data. Under Brazil's data protection law, that list decides what has to be erased when somebody asks. {{lgpd}} Ana erases one customer, and the sales still add up. {{erase}} A catalogue is this, at the size of a company: search, owners, lineage. The idea is the same. The meaning lives next to the data, and a test keeps it true. {{catalogue}}
